claims.claim: UCG 2023 is the current national guideline; its table of contents places hypoglycaemia at 1.1.6 (p. 24), hypertension at 4.1.6 (p. 311), diabetes mellitus at 8.1.3 (p. 471), DKA and HHS at 8.1.4 (p. 478), diabetes in pregnancy at 16.2.5 (p. 711) and diabetic retinopathy at 20.2.3 (p. 936).
claims.population: All patients, all levels of care
claims.document: Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023: National Guidelines for Management of Common Health Conditions (Ministry of Health, Uganda)
claims.section: Title page and table of contents
claims.quote: THE REPUBLIC OF UGANDA / MINISTRY OF HEALTH / Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 / National Guidelines for Management of Common Health Conditions
claims.how_verified: official mirror (National Medical Stores copy): front matter and table of contents opened; body pages not reachable
claims.notes: Page numbers are as relayed from the table of contents by the fetch summariser; the differentiatedservicedelivery.org copy reported p. 469 for 8.1.3 in one read (NMS copy: 471), so confirm pagination against the print copy. MoH landing page https://www.health.go.ug/cause/uganda-clinical-guidelines-2023/ lists 'UCG 2023 Publication (Final PDF Version)', 12 MB. The 'what is new' text seen names Covid-19, self-care, hypoxia management and a palliative care ladder as additions and lists no diabetes-specific change. The user's MoH task force is currently revising UCG 2023.

claims.claim: UCG 2023 codes each treatment with a level of care: HC1 to HC4 are health centres (HC1 is the community level), H is general hospital, RR is regional referral hospital, NR is national referral hospital.

claims.claim: UCG is recalled as a three-step ladder for type 2 diabetes: lifestyle measures plus metformin first; add a sulfonylurea (glibenclamide, or glimepiride at a higher level) if targets are not met after about three months; then add insulin (an evening intermediate-acting NPH insulin, then full insulin regimens), with insulin started from HC IV.

values.second line: add glibenclamide (recalled HC3) or glimepiride (recalled HC4)
values.third line: add NPH insulin, then full insulin regimen (recalled HC4)

claims.conflicts: EMHSLU 2023 deleted glibenclamide and added gliclazide, dapagliflozin and analogue insulins (A1-29, A1-30), so the UCG 2023 ladder names a medicine the national list no longer carries. WHO 2018 guidance and the WHO EML favour gliclazide over glibenclamide; ADA 2026 and KDIGO 2022 put SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists first where there is cardiovascular or kidney disease.

claims.claim: UCG section 1.1.6 is recalled as defining hypoglycaemia as a clinical condition due to reduced blood sugar, with symptoms generally at a blood glucose below 3.0 mmol/L (55 mg/dL); no graded classification is recalled.
claims.population: Adults and children presenting as emergencies
claims.version: 2023 (not opened); recollection is of the 2016 wording, which 2023 largely carries forward
claims.document: Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023: National Guidelines for Management of Common Health Conditions (Ministry of Health, Uganda)

claims.conflicts: ADA 2026 and the International Hypoglycaemia Study Group: level 1 below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL), level 2 below 3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL), level 3 by severity. UCG's own severe malaria text uses below 2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL) (A1-16). WHO paediatric emergency care uses below 2.5 mmol/L, or below 3.0 mmol/L in severe malnutrition. Three different numbers would then sit inside Uganda practice.

claims.quote: Among 2578 included participants, creatinine-based equations overestimated kidney function compared with mGFR, worsened by use of ethnicity coefficients. claims.conflicts: Direction conflicts with the US/European statement in KDIGO 2024 that CKD-EPI 2021 gives 'a small underestimate in Black individuals' - in African populations the error is OVERestimation. Consistent with KDIGO Practice Point 1.2.4.2 (avoid race).

Funding: GSK Africa NCD Open Lab. ENGINE IMPLICATION for Uganda: a creatinine eGFR just above a drug threshold (e.g. 30-45 for metformin, 20-25 for SGLT2i) may truly be below it - display a caution band rather than a hard pass. claims.how_verified: opened primary page
claims.conflicts: Inequality differs by a hair between sources. KDIGO practice point = 'more than 30%' (so exactly 30% continues). KDIGO 2022 Figure 4, on a literal re-check, prints the two branches as '< 30% increase in creatinine' and '> 30% increase in creatinine'. KDIGO 2024 Figure 21 (unofficial mirror, p. S214) prints, on a literal re-check, '<30% decrease in eGFR' and '≥30% decrease in eGFR' - i.e. it switches the variable from creatinine rise to eGFR fall and uses ≥. ADA Rec 11.4d (A): 'Continue renin-angiotensin system blockade for mild to moderate increases in serum creatinine (≤30%) in individuals who have no signs of extracellular fluid volume depletion.' The task brief's '>= 30%' is therefore NOT the wording of the practice point; three of four statements put exactly 30% on the 'continue' side.
claims.notes: A 30% rise in creatinine is not the same quantity as a 30% fall in eGFR (with the CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine exponent of -1.200, a 30% creatinine rise is roughly a 27% eGFR fall - my arithmetic, not from the source) - the engine should implement the practice-point wording on serum creatinine. KDIGO 2024 PP 2.1.4: 'Among people with CKD who initiate hemodynamically active therapies, GFR reductions of >30% on subsequent testing exceed the expected variability and warrant evaluation.' ADA text: 'Elevations in serum creatinine (up to 30% from baseline) with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) blockers (such as ACE inhibitors and ARBs) must not be confused with AKI.' The final figure box in KDIGO 2022 Figure 4 reads 'Reduce dose or stop ACEi or ARB'; KDIGO 2024 Figure 21 adds 'if mitigation strategies ineffective'.

claims.quote: Diabetes doubles the chances of having glaucoma, which can lead to vision loss and blindness if not treated early. ... People with diabetes can develop cataracts at an earlier age than people without diabetes.
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (NIDDK)
claims.conflicts: Optometry Australia lists 'Higher incidence of open-angle glaucoma' and 'Neovascular glaucoma' (rubeosis) separately - the latter is a complication of proliferative disease.
claims.notes: Public-information page from a US government institute, not a graded guideline. Two sentences joined by an ellipsis. Engine flag: painful red eye with PDR = possible neovascular glaucoma (urgent) - design note.

claims.claim: High blood glucose can change fluid levels or cause swelling in the focusing tissues of the eye, causing temporary blurred vision.

values.mechanism: fluid shifts/swelling of the focusing tissues (lens)
values.course: temporary; resolves as glucose approaches normal

claims.population: People with diabetes with hyperglycaemia or changing treatment
claims.document: Diabetic Eye Disease (NIDDK health information)
claims.quote: High glucose can change fluid levels or cause swelling in the tissues of your eyes that help you to focus, causing blurred vision.
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (NIDDK)
claims.notes: No graded guideline statement on osmotic lens/refractive shift was found in ADA 2026 Section 12, ICO 2017 or WHO 2020; this is a patient-level statement from an official body. Engine: blurred vision at presentation with marked hyperglycaemia should be labelled 'likely refractive - recheck after glucose stabilises' but must NOT suppress eye referral if VA stays worse than 6/12 or other symptoms exist (design note).

claims.claim: AAO: rapid blood-sugar changes alter lens shape and blur vision, which returns to normal once blood sugar stabilises; have blood sugar controlled before the spectacle prescription is checked.

values.advice: defer refraction/spectacle prescription until blood glucose is controlled

claims.version: American Academy of Ophthalmology patient education page (undated in extraction)
claims.document: Diabetic Eye Disease (American Academy of Ophthalmology, EyeSmart)
claims.quote: If your blood sugar levels change quickly, it can affect the shape of your eye's lens, causing blurry vision. Your vision goes back to normal after your blood sugar stabilizes. Have your blood sugar controlled before getting your eyeglasses prescription checked.
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (aao.org)
claims.notes: Patient-education text from a professional body, not a graded recommendation; no number of weeks is given (textbooks commonly say several weeks - from memory, unverified). Optometry Australia Appendix D lists 'Refractive error changes' and 'Accommodative dysfunction' as functional complications. CSO to supply a citable interval if the engine is to display one.

claims.claim: Diabetes can cause mononeuropathies of the third, fourth or sixth cranial nerves (extraocular muscle palsy, diplopia).
claims.document: Optometry Australia Guidelines for the Examination and Management of Patients with Diabetes
claims.section: Appendix D: Ocular and Visual Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
claims.quote: Extraocular muscle anomalies: Mononeuropathies involving third, fourth, or sixth cranial nerves
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (Optometry Australia PDF)
claims.conflicts: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 12 (retinopathy and neuropathy narrative) contains no sentence on cranial nerves, mononeuropathy or diplopia.
claims.notes: From memory, NOT verified: the ADA position statement 'Diabetic Neuropathy' (Pop-Busui R et al., Diabetes Care 2017;40:136-154) Table 1 classifies 'Mononeuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex) (atypical forms): isolated cranial or peripheral nerve (e.g., CN III, ulnar, median, femoral, peroneal)'. Clinical teaching that a diabetic third-nerve palsy is typically pupil-sparing and recovers over about 3 months is from memory and unverified; a pupil-involving III palsy needs urgent imaging. Same Appendix D also lists papillopathy, ischaemic optic neuropathy, reduced corneal sensitivity, dry eye, rubeosis iridis.

claims.claim: Pooled prevalence of diabetic retinopathy among people with diabetes in sub-Saharan Africa is about 25.5%, highest in East Africa (31.8%).
claims.population: People with diabetes in sub-Saharan Africa
claims.document: Ismail MF, Khalafalla I, Sheck ZO, et al. Diabetic retinopathy in Sub-Saharan Africa: prevalence and regional variations from a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Ophthalmology 2025;26:53
claims.quote: The overall pooled prevalence of DR among individuals with diabetes was 25.5% (95% CI: 20.7%-31.0%)
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (Springer/BMC)
claims.conflicts: WHO 2020 short guide: 20-35% any DR. Uganda-only pooled estimate 19.5% (Kibirige 2026). East Africa pooled 28% (Abuhay 2025).
claims.notes: Regional figures quoted in the abstract: 'East Africa 31.8%, Southern Africa 29.6%, West Africa 27.4%, and Central Africa 13.7%'. Includes one Ugandan study (Magan et al., 2019, Mulago). Volume/article number as returned by the extraction (2025;26:53) should be checked.

claims.claim: Pooled prevalence of diabetic retinopathy among adults with diabetes in East African countries is 28%.
claims.population: Adults with diabetes in East Africa
claims.document: Abuhay HW, Tesfie TK, Alemayehu MA, et al. Prevalence of diabetic retinopathy and its associated factors among adults in East African countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLOS ONE 2025;20(1):e0316160
claims.quote: Among the 29 included studies, the estimated pooled prevalence of DR in East African countries was 28% (95% CI 23.0, 33.0).
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (PLOS ONE)
claims.notes: Two Ugandan studies included; no Uganda-specific subgroup estimate reported.

claims.claim: Pooled prevalence of diabetic retinopathy among adult Ugandans with diabetes is 19.5% (seven studies, very high heterogeneity).
claims.document: Kibirige D, Olum R, Turyamureeba W, et al. Prevalence and factors associated with microvascular and macrovascular diabetes complications in adult Ugandans: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLOS ONE 2026;21(6):e0312792
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (PLOS ONE)
claims.conflicts: Lower than the SSA (25.5%) and East Africa (28-31.8%) pooled estimates; the wide CI reflects few, heterogeneous, mostly clinic-based studies and probable under-ascertainment where no dilated exam was done. Matovu 2024 states the national prevalence 'is unknown'. Makeri 2026 (Health Sciences Review 18:100253) reports 'visual impairment 28 % (95 % CI: 14.0-49.0)' among Ugandans with diabetes.
claims.notes: Best single Uganda figure, but should be presented with its CI.

claims.claim: Burgess 2013 systematic review: in African population-based studies DR prevalence in people with diabetes was 30.2-31.6%, PDR 0.9-1.3%, maculopathy 1.2-4.5%; clinic-based ranges were much wider.
claims.document: Burgess PI, MacCormick IJC, Harding SP, Bastawrous A, Beare NAV, Garner P. Epidemiology of diabetic retinopathy and maculopathy in Africa: a systematic review. Diabetic Medicine 2013;30(4):399-412
claims.section: Abstract (as reproduced on Sightsavers evidence gap map)
claims.quote: In population based studies the prevalence range in patients with diabetes for diabetic retinopathy was 30.2% to 31.6%, proliferative diabetic retinopathy 0.9% to 1.3% and any maculopathy 1.2% to 4.5%.
claims.how_verified: official summary page reproducing the abstract (Wiley page returned 403; Europe PMC blocked by robots)
claims.notes: Clinic-based sentence: 'In clinic-based surveys, the reported prevalence range for diabetic retinopathy was 7.0% to 62.4%, proliferative diabetic retinopathy 0% to 6.9% and any maculopathy 1.2% to 31.1%.'

claims.claim: Uganda TADDS assessment (2024): 95% of stakeholders reported no community DR screening programmes; the country had 51 ophthalmologists and five vitreoretinal surgeons, mostly in Kampala.
claims.document: Matovu JKB, Kakinda M, Bubikire S, Kilberg K, Mariotti SP. Stakeholders' perspectives on the status of diabetic retinopathy and diabetes health service management systems in Uganda. Discover Health Systems 2024. doi 10.1007/s44250-024-00121-6
claims.quote: 95% (n = 36) reported that there are no community screening programs for DR.
claims.how_verified: opened primary page (Springer)

Other verbatim fragments: '51 Ophthalmologists, 15 Optometrists and five (5) Vitreoretinal Surgeons'; 'Of the four Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) machines available to diagnose DR in Uganda, three are based in Kampala'; 'the prevalence of DR is unknown'. The paper says DR management guidance is 'contained in the 2016 Uganda Clinical Guidelines'. Screening coverage is therefore opportunistic; the engine recall list is the de facto register.

values.mild_NPDR: Micro aneurysms only - refer to retina clinic; follow-up in 12 months
values.moderate_NPDR: more than just aneurysms but less than severe NPDR - refer to retina clinic; follow-up 6-12 months
values.severe_NPDR: refer to retina clinic; review in 6 months or consider pan retinal laser if follow-up unreliable
values.PDR: urgent referral to retina clinic; PRP / vitrectomy if vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment

values.ME_severe: affecting centre of fovea - refer; laser or intravitreal anti-VEGF

claims.claim: UK NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme grades R0-R3 and M0/M1; higher-risk pre-proliferative (R2H) is defined by the ICDR 4-2-1 rule and must always be referred to hospital eye services.

values.R0: no DR (isolated cotton wool spots without microaneurysm/haemorrhage count as no DR)
values.R1: background: microaneurysms, retinal haemorrhages, any exudate
values.R2: pre-proliferative: multiple blot haemorrhages, IRMA, venous beading, venous reduplication; split into R2L and R2H
values.R2H: > 20 intraretinal haemorrhages/microaneurysms in each of four quadrants; venous beading in two or more quadrants; moderate IRMA >= ETDRS standard photograph 8a in one or more quadrants
values.M1: includes VA <= 6/12 with microaneurysms or haemorrhages within one disc diameter of the centre of the fovea; group of exudates >= half disc area within the macula

[...] causes of neuropathy other than diabetes should be considered, including toxins (e.g., alcohol), neurotoxic medications (e.g., chemotherapy), vitamin B12 (especially in those treated chronically with metformin) [...] hypothyroidism, kidney disease, malignancies [...], infections (e.g., HIV, hepatitis C)

claims.notes: Quote abridged at each [...] to fit 400 characters. Omitted text, in order: 'In all people with diabetes and DPN,'; 'and other nutritional deficiencies (e.g., acquired copper deficiency after metabolic surgery),'; '(e.g., multiple myeloma, bronchogenic carcinoma)'; and the sentence ends ', chronic inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy, inherited neuropathies, and vasculitis'. UGANDA: ADA names chemotherapy as its only example of a neurotoxic drug - it does NOT name isoniazid. Isoniazid (TB treatment and TB preventive therapy in people with HIV), older ART (stavudine/didanosine) and HIV itself are the locally dominant non-diabetic causes; that addition is clinical context, not an ADA statement, and needs CSO sign-off before it enters the engine.
